<reason>Both sides were excellent and disciplined, but A built the more durable path. A set and held the debate's central question — why does a model that benefits everyone collapse when permission is asked — and neutralized more of B's opening: "existing tools" was met with two decades of enforcement failure and "you cannot sue over a job ad you never saw"; entrenchment was reversed ("the moat is the trove"); the grocer/supermarket analogies were confined to first-party data. B fought back superbly with the rational-ignorance answer, the "three statutes from the podium" attack, and a sharp closing dilemma, and deserves credit for unusually honest, direct A1/A2 answers. But B's core economic route (opt-in kills the free web) rested on asserted magnitude claims A plausibly contested with substitutes; its proportionality close was answered by A's "smallness never licensed taking" and the aggregation argument; and its clipped second rebuttal is a real execution cost. A's final crystallization — converting friction, pennies, and rational ignorance into the reason individuals cannot carry the opt-out burden — gave the cleaner reason to vote.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The frictionless-consent sequence: A's Q1 forced B to concede opt-in stays low even when asking is genuinely easy; B answered honestly with the rational-ignorance/pennies defense, but A's closing converted that concession into the case for the presumption — diffuse penny-scale harms are exactly why opt-out enforcement cannot work and the default must flip. A2.4's "you cannot sue over a job ad you never saw" was the runner-up, gutting B's existing-tools route early.</best_rebuttal>
